```{python}
#| include: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (MSTL, AutoETS, AutoTheta, HistoricAverage,
                                  Naive, RandomWalkWithDrift, SeasonalNaive)
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox

import coursekit
from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P
from coursekit import scoring

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()

# The whole board, measured here rather than read off labs/leaderboard.csv, so
# this deck renders the same whether or not anyone has run the labs yet.
BOARD = [("HistoricAverage", "Mean", 2), ("Naive", "Naive", 2),
         ("SeasonalNaive", "Seasonal naive", 2), ("RWD", "Drift", 2),
         ("MSTL", "STL + drift", 2), ("AutoETS", "ETS", 3),
         ("AutoARIMA", "ARIMA", 3), ("AutoTheta", "Theta", 3)]
LABELS = {col: label for col, label, _ in BOARD}

# Everything except AutoARIMA is cheap enough to fit while the deck renders.
sf = StatsForecast(
    models=[HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
            RandomWalkWithDrift(),
            MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift()),
            AutoETS(season_length=12), AutoTheta(season_length=12)],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
cv = sf.cross_validation(df=spine, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=8,
                         level=scoring.LEVELS)
score = {col: scoring.score_cv(cv, col, spine)
         for col, _, _ in BOARD if col != "AutoARIMA"}

# AutoARIMA is the exception: an order search plus eight folds is about 100
# seconds, which is too slow to repeat on every render of this deck. It is
# measured once by scripts/measure_arima.py and committed, so these numbers are
# measured rather than typed. Re-run that script if the spine, the fold layout
# or scoring.LEVELS ever changes.
arima = json.loads(
    (Path(coursekit.__file__).parent / "data" / "day3_arima.json")
    .read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
ARIMA_SPEC = arima["spec"]
score["AutoARIMA"] = {k: arima[k] for k in
                      ("mase", "rmsse", "crps", "coverage_80",
                       "mase_min", "mase_max")}

board = (pd.DataFrame([{"model": label, "day": day, **score[col]}
                       for col, label, day in BOARD])
         .sort_values("crps").reset_index(drop=True))

# --- the Day 2 hook this deck closes: seasonal naive residuals -------------
sn = StatsForecast(models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12)], freq=D.FREQ,
                   n_jobs=1)
sn.forecast(df=spine, h=1, fitted=True)
fv = sn.forecast_fitted_values()
sn_resid = (fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]).dropna()
LB_P = float(acorr_ljungbox(sn_resid, lags=[24],
                            return_df=True)["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0])

THREE = ["SeasonalNaive", "AutoETS", "AutoARIMA"]
cover = {m: score[m]["coverage_80"] for m in score}
crps = {m: score[m]["crps"] for m in score}
mase = {m: score[m]["mase"] for m in score}
```

# A. The other classical family {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 9 · One slide, one call, and one promise kept

## Your residuals said there was structure left

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
P.acf_plot(sn_resid, nlags=24,
           title="Seasonal naive residuals, and they are not white noise")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
Ljung-Box on 24 lags: $p \approx$ `{python} f"{LB_P:.0e}"`. Yesterday this was
the reason to keep going. Nothing since has picked that structure up.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that pays off a debt. On Day 2 they ran Ljung-Box on the
seasonal naive's residuals, got a p-value with 245 zeros in front of it, and
were told that the structure it proves is the opening for Day 3.

Then this morning ETS did not take it. ETS tied the floor. So the honest state
of play, right now, is that the promise is still outstanding.

Point at the bars that cross the bound. Those are the autocorrelations a model
of this series ought to be using and the seasonal naive throws away: last
month's error tells you something about this month's, and nothing in the
benchmark family has any machinery for saying so.

The family that does have that machinery is ARIMA, and specifically its MA
half, which forecasts the next value partly from the last few errors.
:::

## ARIMA models the errors the benchmarks discard

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**AR** · the next value from the last few **values**

**MA** · the next value from the last few **errors**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**I** · difference the series until it is stationary

**Seasonal orders** · the same three, one year apart
:::
::::

. . .

`AutoARIMA` searches that space the way `AutoETS` searched its own, and on the
spine it picks `{python} ARIMA_SPEC`.

::: {.notes}
Four ideas, one slide, and deliberately no derivation. This is the only slide
of ARIMA in the course and the goal is that the vocabulary is not foreign when
they meet it, not that they can select orders by hand.

Read the selected model aloud and unpack the notation once, because it is worth
being able to read: the first bracket is the non-seasonal part, the second is
the seasonal part, and the 12 is the season length. The D of 1 is a seasonal
difference, which is the model saying what Day 1 said with a seasonal plot.

Note the MA term in both brackets. That is the piece that consumes the
autocorrelation on the previous slide, and it is exactly what the benchmark
family lacks.

If someone asks what differencing is: subtract the previous value, or the value
twelve months back, until the series stops trending. Stationarity is the
assumption underneath the whole family. That is as far as this course goes.
:::

## One call, sixty seconds, and the promise kept

```python
from statsforecast.models import AutoARIMA

sf = StatsForecast(models=[AutoARIMA(season_length=12)], freq="MS")
cv = sf.cross_validation(df=spine, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=8,
                         level=scoring.LEVELS)
lb.record("ARIMA", day=3, **scoring.score_cv(cv, "AutoARIMA", spine))
```

. . .

| | Seasonal naive | ETS | ARIMA |
|---|---|---|---|
| MASE | `{python} f"{mase['SeasonalNaive']:.3f}"` | `{python} f"{mase['AutoETS']:.3f}"` | **`{python} f"{mase['AutoARIMA']:.3f}"`** |
| Scaled CRPS | **`{python} f"{crps['SeasonalNaive']:.4f}"`** | `{python} f"{crps['AutoETS']:.4f}"` | `{python} f"{crps['AutoARIMA']:.4f}"` |

::: {.notes}
Same six lines as this morning, one word changed. That is the third time today
the harness has taken a new model without modification, and it is worth naming
again because Part B is about what you give up when a framework owns that step.

The cross-validation takes about a minute. Say so before you run it, and use
the pause: this is the first model in the course whose fitting time is
noticeable, and eight folds of order search is where it goes.

The result is the best MASE of the three. ARIMA did find structure that the
seasonal naive and ETS both missed, which is the promise from yesterday kept.

And it still loses on CRPS. Hold that; the next slide is about why.
:::

## Two models, two opposite ways to be wrong

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
P.coverage_bars({LABELS[m]: cover[m] for m in THREE}, nominal=0.8,
                tolerance=0.05, figsize=(8.6, 2.9),
                title="Measured 80% coverage over 8 folds")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cardbox .navy}
ETS covers `{python} f"{cover['AutoETS']:.1%}"` with a band claiming 80%.
ARIMA covers `{python} f"{cover['AutoARIMA']:.1%}"`. One is too wide, the
other too narrow, and both lose to the benchmark on CRPS.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the Day 2 lesson confirmed from both sides at once, and it is the most
useful slide of the afternoon.

ETS over-covers, which reads as caution and costs money in hedging. ARIMA
under-covers, which is the failure that actually hurts: a band that claims 80
percent and delivers 62 will surprise you roughly twice as often as your
planning assumed, and every one of those surprises is a stockout or an overrun.

Ask which failure they would rather explain to a stakeholder. Neither answer is
wrong; the point is that they are different failures with different costs, and
coverage is the only thing that tells them apart.

Then close the loop: the seasonal naive is not on top here because it is
clever. Its band is roughly the right size and roughly in the right place, and
nothing in the last two days has managed to be both.
:::

# B. Handing the fitting step over {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

AutoGluon TimeSeries · the orchestrated layer

## A framework is a parallel API universe

::: {.flowrow}
[[Your frame]{.flowtitle}[`unique_id` · `ds` · `y`]{.flownote}]{.flownode .navy}
[[Their frame]{.flowtitle}[`TimeSeriesDataFrame`]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[Their fit loop]{.flowtitle}[a zoo, a budget, an ensemble]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[Their leaderboard]{.flowtitle}[scores with the sign flipped]{.flownote}]{.flownode .purple}
:::

. . .

Every stage is a model you have built. None of the plumbing is.

::: {.notes}
Set the expectation for the lab before any code appears. AutoGluon is not a
model, it is an orchestration layer, and it brings its own everything: its own
frame type, its own column names, its own fit loop, its own leaderboard with
its own sign convention.

That is the thing to notice this afternoon. The forecasting content of the tool
is a subset of what they already have. The cost of adopting it is entirely in
the second row of that flow, the plumbing, and the benefit is entirely in the
third.

Tell them the data conversion stays visible in the notebook on purpose. A
coursekit helper could hide it in one line, and hiding it would delete the only
lesson this exercise has.
:::

## The conversion is two renames and a constructor

| | this course | AutoGluon |
|---|---|---|
| series id | `unique_id` | `item_id` |
| timestamp | `ds` | `timestamp` |
| value | `y` | `target`, nameable |
| container | `pd.DataFrame` | `TimeSeriesDataFrame` |

```python
ag_long = spine.rename(columns={"unique_id": "item_id", "ds": "timestamp"})
tsdf = TimeSeriesDataFrame.from_data_frame(
    ag_long, id_column="item_id", timestamp_column="timestamp")
```

::: {.notes}
Two renames and a constructor. That is the entire conceptual content of the
conversion, and it is worth showing precisely because it is so thin: the long
format this course has used since the first hour is the format every serious
forecasting library expects, under different column names.

Say the general lesson, since it outlives this library. When you meet a new
forecasting tool, the first question is what it calls the three columns and
whether it wants one frame or many. If the answer is long format, which it
almost always is, you already know how to feed it.

The `slice_by_timestep` call in the notebook is how AutoGluon cuts a holdout.
It is their `train_test`, with a different name.
:::

so the run stops when it stops.

Warn them again about the runtime reset wiping the install.

## Its leaderboard is not ours

::: {.callout-important}
## Every AutoGluon score is negated
Higher is better there. Lower is better on our board. A `score_val` of
$-1.18$ is a MASE of `{python} f"{mase['SeasonalNaive']:.2f}"`.
:::

. . .

| | course leaderboard | AutoGluon leaderboard |
|---|---|---|
| sign | lower is better | **higher** is better |
| windows | 8 rolling folds | one internal validation split |
| distribution | scaled CRPS | its own weighted quantile loss |

::: {.notes}
This slide exists because the sign flip catches everybody, including people who
have used the library for months. When a framework's ranking disagrees with
yours, check the sign before you check anything else.

The second and third rows matter more for the exercise. AutoGluon scored one
internal validation window; the course board averages eight rolling folds and
scores the whole distribution. So the two tables can legitimately disagree
about the ranking without either being wrong.

That is Exercise 2.5 pointed at a tool instead of a model, and it is why the
course table is the one to trust for a production decision. A framework's
default validation is a convenience, not an evaluation protocol.

They will also see a `WeightedEnsemble` row that beats its members. That is
Part C's last line arriving early.
:::

## What the framework buys, and what it does not

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Buys**

Five models fitted, tuned and ensembled inside one call and a fixed budget.
Scale to many series without new code.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Does not buy**

An evaluation protocol you trust. A reason to prefer the winner. Any way to
know a band is too wide.
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
You have now seen every line this library runs. In industry you hand this step
to a framework, and you still own the judgement.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the thesis of the day, so land it slowly.

The left column is real and should not be undersold. Orchestration is genuinely
valuable, and on 148 series rather than one it is not optional. Nobody should
leave thinking the course disapproves of AutoGluon.

The right column is what the last three days were for. The framework will
always return a winner. It will not tell you whether the winner is better than
a seasonal naive, whether its intervals are honest, or whether the margin
survives a second window. Those are the questions, and they are yours.

The card is the line to close on. Say it, then hand over to the map.
:::

# C. The field, and where to go next {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Listed, not taught · one line each

## Four more classical families, by name

::: {.incremental}
- **Theta** · simple, fast, strong. In AutoGluon's zoo, and best on this series
- **ARIMA** · Ch 9, one slide ago. The other classical family
- **Dynamic regression** · Ch 7 and 10, for when you have price or promotions
- **Hierarchical** · Ch 11, when state totals must equal the national total
:::

::: {.notes}
Four names, one line each, and no apology for the brevity. The purpose of the
map is recognition: when one of these turns up in a paper or a job spec, they
should know roughly what it is and where to read about it.

Theta first, because it is the one they will meet in the capstone in twenty
minutes and because it makes an honest point about complexity. It is a very
simple method and it is about to win the whole board.

Dynamic regression is the one most likely to matter in their actual work.
Everything this course did used only the series' own past. The moment you have
a price, a promotion calendar or a holiday flag, that is the chapter. Note that
Ch 10 is really Ch 7 plus Ch 9, so regression travels with it.

Hierarchical is worth naming for anyone forecasting a business with regions or
product lines, which is most of them.
:::

## Where machine learning enters the field

::: {.incremental}
- **Lag-feature ML** · LightGBM with `mlforecast`; a tabular framing, no fpppy chapter
- **Neural** · DeepAR, Transformers. Global models, and they want many series
- **Foundation models** · Chronos, Moirai, TimeGPT. Zero-shot, no fitting
- **Ensembles** · combine forecasts; AutoGluon's `WeightedEnsemble` is one
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .purple}
Every one of these still gets scored by the harness you built. That is the part
that transfers.
:::

::: {.notes}
The second half of the map, and the half with the most hype attached, so keep
the tone level.

Lag features are how most working data scientists actually do this: build a
tabular frame of lags and rolling statistics, then fit a gradient booster.
fpppy has no chapter on it. Warn them once about the trap Day 2 covered, which
is computing a feature over data the fold was not allowed to see.

Neural models are global: one model across many series, learning shared
structure. On one series with 441 points they are the wrong tool, which is
worth saying plainly because the instinct runs the other way.

Foundation models are the genuinely new thing. Pretrained, and they forecast a
series they have never seen with no fitting at all. On Colab, Chronos-Bolt-small
or Moirai-small run on CPU; TimeGPT needs an API key and Moirai needs weights
from Hugging Face.

Ensembles last, because it is the cheapest reliable win in forecasting and the
least glamorous.
:::

## Choosing, in practice

:::: {.flowconv}
::: {.flowcauses}
[[One series]{.flowtitle}[benchmarks, then ETS]{.flownote}]{.flownode .teal}
[[Many, related]{.flowtitle}[global ML or neural]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[Drivers to use]{.flowtitle}[dynamic regression]{.flownote}]{.flownode .purple}
:::
[[Score them the same way]{.flowtitle}[rolling folds, a proper score]{.flownote}]{.flownode .navy}
::::

. . .

The first move on any new series is still the benchmark floor.

::: {.notes}
If the room remembers one slide of Part C, this is the one to make it.

The three inputs at the top are the questions that actually decide the family:
how many series, how related they are, and whether you have anything to
regress on. Everything else is detail.

The bottom node is the part that does not change with the family, and it is
what the course was really about. A neural model and a seasonal naive get
scored by the same harness, over the same folds, on the same proper score, or
you cannot compare them at all.

Then the closing line, which should sound almost too simple by now: fit the
benchmarks first. The next slide is why.
:::

## The floor held, and one thing beat it

::: {.callout-tip}
## The closing result
Theta wins on MASE and on scaled CRPS, in three lines and with no lecture.
Nothing else beat the seasonal naive on the distribution.
:::

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- A one-line benchmark survived a full day of fitted models
- Complexity did not order the board; honest uncertainty did
- You cannot know which is which without a harness
:::

::: {.notes}
Two things to land, and they pull in opposite directions on purpose.

First, the floor held. Across ETS, ARIMA and the decomposition route, only
Theta beat a model that takes one line and no fitting time. This is why the
benchmark floor is the first thing you build on a new series. Not as a
formality. As the thing that most of your candidates will fail to beat.

Second, the winner is the simple one. Theta is simpler than ETS and beat it.
ARIMA is more complex than both and lost. If complexity ordered forecast
accuracy, this board would read the other way around.

What did order it was whether each model's uncertainty was priced honestly, and
that is not visible from the model, only from the evaluation. Which is the
third bullet, and the whole point of Day 2.

Then hand to the lab: they are about to reproduce this table themselves, and
the capstone is where Theta shows up.
:::
